title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
hookLine: two old people who waited their whole lives hold the child and say now I can go in peace
tomorrow: who follows a star to meet a stranger's baby?
last: GOOD NEWS GOES TO THE OUTSIDERS FIRST.

lines: FORTY DAYS OLD, AT THE TEMPLE.
cards: Loading bars. Waiting rooms. The three dots that say someone's typing, then vanish.
Waiting can feel like dead time, the part of life you'd skip if you could. Luke tells about two people who waited most of their lives for one moment.

Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby to the Temple in Jerusalem with two birds, the offering the law allowed families who couldn't afford a lamb. Nobody notices one more young couple. Almost nobody.

teach.b: The question is old: is waiting wasted? Luke answers with two people. Simeon is just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit has promised he won't die before he sees the Messiah.
How long he waited, Luke doesn't say.

That day he's moved to go to the Temple, takes the child in his arms, and prays, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." I can go now; I've seen it.
He calls the child "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel," then warns Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul.
Then Anna, a prophetess, widowed after seven years of marriage, a widow into her eighties, who never left the Temple, praying and fasting night and day. Her waiting wasn't empty. It was full.
So the answer here: waiting done like that is a way of watching, and it's why these two knew a baby everyone else walked past.

teach.h: ANNA: A WAITING FULL OF PRAYER.
teach.b: Simeon and Anna were Jews waiting on Israel's hope, and that waiting still runs through Jewish prayer: a creed built on the principles of Maimonides says, in effect, though he tarry, I will wait for him every day.
Catholics pray Simeon's words every night at Night Prayer, called the Nunc Dimittis from its Latin.
And because he called the child a light, candles are blessed on this feast, February 2: Candlemas.

how: Catholics celebrate the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, blessing candles at Mass (Candlemas); Simeon's prayer, the Nunc Dimittis, is said every night at Night Prayer.

o: the Latin words a priest says to dismiss Mass
Simeon's prayer: let your servant go now in peace
a prayer for the dying said at a deathbed vigil

games.q: who's in the Temple — tap the pairs.
p: praying and fasting night and day
the offering of a poor family

s: Simeon was the Temple's high priest
Luke calls him just and devout, never a priest. later art sometimes dressed him as one.
Luke tells us exactly how long Simeon waited
he doesn't. only that he'd been promised he wouldn't die first.
candles are blessed on this feast because Simeon called the child a light

games.q: your grandpa has waited months for a surgery date and calls it "dead time." what does the Simeon and Anna story offer him?
o: proof that good things come quickly if you believe.
waiting can be watching: Anna filled hers with prayer.
advice to stop waiting and get on with life.
games.why: Simeon waited years and Anna decades, and neither waiting was empty: they watched, prayed, and recognized the moment when it came.

practice: Close your eyes and sit beside something you've waited a long time for: healing, a person, a change, an answer. Don't push it away or grab at it; just sit with it, the way Anna sat in the Temple.
If Simeon's words are yours, let them be the last thing before you open your eyes: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace.

wordCard.voice: Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's prayer, said every night, from a man whose waiting was over.

orig.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the first words of Simeon's prayer, said nightly at Compline.

carryVoice: Your line: waiting is not wasted. Simeon and Anna spent theirs watching. Go in peace.
